transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-06-12
- Start: 14:00 PDT, Duration: ~52m
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Aaron (Redwood SE), David (CTO, Helion), Priya (Head of ML), Carlos (SRE)

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE run a discovery focused on latency and throughput requirements for Helion Finance. Customer has a high-throughput inference use case (real-time fraud scoring + personalized messaging) and is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. Main questions: p95 targets for short/long prompts, concurrency behavior, streaming first-byte latency, token/sec sustainable throughput, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2). SE agrees to run token/sec benchmark with customer's prompts and propose Dedicated capacity sizing.

Topics:
- Intro / context and current infra (0:00)
- p95 SLOs and observability needs (6:20)
- Streaming vs non-streaming behaviour (14:05)
- Benchmarking approach and next steps (28:40)
- Security and private deployment questions (36:10)
- Recap & action items (48:30)

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to go through latency and throughput requirements and see how Redwood fits. a quick round of intros?
[00:08] David: david here CTO at Helion, we run payments and realtime risk, our latencies matter a lot, thanks for doing this.
[00:15] Priya: priya, head of ml, i'll own model evals and prompt sets.
[00:19] Carlos: carlos, SRE, i'll be focused on capacity and networking — vpc stuff.
[00:25] Aaron: great, i'm a se on inference side. quick agenda: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, benchmark plan.
[00:33] Maya: super. david can you give a little context on current stack and what you're measuring today?
[00:38] David: yeah so we currently host models on managed k8s with tf-serving and a mix of g4/h100 instances for batch scoring; but for customer-facing features we've seen p95 spikes during promo bursts. target is p95 under 400ms for short prompts (<=256 tokens) and for longer prompts we want p95 under 1.2s at 512 tokens, ideally better. our concurrency peak in peak traffic windows is ~120 concurrent inference streams for the fraud flow and another 30 for personalization.
[01:10] Aaron: ok that helps. to confirm: p95 400ms for <=256 tokens is pretty aggressive depending on the model size and deployment mode, but achievable with dedicated pools and streaming optimizations for smaller models. is that 400ms end-to-end or server-side?
[01:23] David: end-to-end from our API to response first payload — includes network; we can isolate server-side numbers during bench.
[01:30] Priya: also note our prompts vary — some are short structured prompts for scoring, some are 1.5–2k token prompts for customer summaries. throughput requirements differ.
[01:40] Aaron: makes sense. a couple of clarifications: for streaming the first-byte latency (ttfb) and token generation rate matter. we typically see first byte in 80–200ms on optimized infra for small models, and sustained token rates of 40–80 tokens/sec on H100-ish backends for medium models; for larger 70B+ models token/sec can be under 10–20. so we need to map your model choices.
[02:05] David: we're evaluating a 13B/70B mix; scoring uses a tuned 13B quantized model, summaries use 70B. scoring is latency-sensitive.
[02:14] Aaron: ok that aligns — for scoring on 13B quantized (4-bit) on dedicated pool we can get p95 single-request server-side under ~150–250ms for short prompts and streaming first byte under 120ms in many cases, depending on sequence length and KV cache hit rates. network + app overhead tends to add 50–100ms.
[02:32] Carlos: when you say dedicated pool, what does that look like? how many gpus, autoscaling, can we pin instances?
[02:38] Maya: Redwood Dedicated is reserved GPU pools, you can configure sizes, autoscale policies, burst capacity. we can allocate pinned nodes for SRE isolation; autoscaling is configurable with warm standby to avoid cold-start latency.
[02:50] Carlos: do you support private deployment (VPC) and KMS integration? we need customer-managed keys and audit logs.
[02:56] Maya: yes Redwood Private provides VPC/on-prem options, KMS/HSM integration, SAML SSO, audit logs, SOC2. we'll share the security pack.
[03:05] Priya: in terms of benchmarks how do you run them? we need token/sec numbers on our actual prompts, not synthetic.
[03:11] Aaron: agreed — best practice is to run your representative prompt set across target model variants and sim concurrency to measure p50/p95/p99 for first byte and end-to-end completion. we can run streaming and non-streaming (batch) tests. we'll collect tokens/sec sustained per GPU and end-to-end QPS for pool sizes.
[03:28] Priya: what's typical tokens/sec per GPU for 13B quantized vs 70B? just ballpark.
[03:33] Aaron: ballpark: 13B quantized (4-bit) on H100 getting ~150–300 tokens/sec single-stream (higher with batching), 70B distilled variants might be ~20–60 tokens/sec. these vary a lot with max sequence and whether KV cache hits are used. with prefix/KV caching for repeated context we see effective token/sec improve because you avoid recomputing earlier tokens.
[03:55] David: we need p95 for scoring under 400ms including network; could we do hosted with that SLAs or must we go dedicated/private?
[04:02] Maya: hosted can achieve it for many cases but at high concurrency and strict SLOs dedicated is recommended — predictable throughput and data isolation. private gives max control but has more ops burden.
[04:12] Carlos: do you have fallbacks if capacity spikes — e.g., degrade to smaller model or region?
[04:17] Aaron: yes smart routing and automatic fallback policies — canary or A/B rollouts. we can route by latency/cost and fallback to cheaper variants when pool is saturated.
[04:26] Maya: one common approach is hybrid: scoring on Redwood Dedicated with autoscaling + burst, summaries on hosted or larger dedicated pool.
[04:33] Priya: what's the impact of streaming on p95? we want first token fast so UI can show typing.
[04:38] Aaron: streaming reduces perceived latency; first byte is the key metric. p95 for first-byte on streaming is usually lower than full completion p95 since you don't wait for model to finish. typical first-byte p95 numbers we aim for: <=120–250ms for short prompts on dedicated, full completion p95 depends on token count and tokens/sec.
[04:58] David: ok good to know. for the POC we'd like you to run a token/sec benchmark with our 2k token prompt (summary) at 50 concurrent users and a separate 512-token scoring benchmark at 120 concurrent users.
[05:10] Aaron: sounds good — for the 120 concurrent scoring traffic we should simulate both cold-cache and warm-cache (KV cache) scenarios — the warm-cache case will be much faster, often 30–60% lower latency.
[05:23] Priya: can you explain cache hit rates and how Redwood handles prefix caching?
[05:27] Aaron: sure — we support automatic prefix/KV caching at runtime; if requests share a prefix (e.g., same user context) the KV cache avoids recomputing earlier layers. we also support client-side caching patterns. cache eviction and consistency are configurable.
[05:40] Carlos: network wise we need VPC peering and private endpoints; is that supported for hosted?
[05:45] Maya: hosted supports private endpoints for enterprise tiers; for full VPC isolation we recommend Redwood Private. both support customer KMS integration.
[05:52] David: what about multi-region failover? we need 99.95% availability and failover to secondary region under 30s for critical path.
[05:58] Aaron: Redwood supports region routing and automated fallback; Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and can be configured across regions with warm standby nodes. failover time depends on DNS and routing but we can push to under 30s with health checks and routing policies.
[06:12] Priya: do you provide per-route token-level breakdowns for cost/latency?
[06:15] Maya: yes Redwood Console has per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, traces and error analysis, and eval hooks.
[06:22] David: can you give examples of sizing? what does 120 concurrent scoring look like in GPUs?
[06:28] Aaron: rough example: for 13B quantized with average 100-token responses, 120 concurrent sustained requesters with target p95 ~200–400ms might need a small cluster of say 4–8 H100s with autoscale; exact depends on batching, token/sec, and whether requests are bursty. we'll run an internal sim.
[06:50] Carlos: what's batching behavior — do you automatically batch requests and how does that affect latency?
[06:54] Aaron: Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with latency-aware thresholds. batching improves throughput (tokens/sec) but can increase tail latency if you wait to fill a batch. we tune batch windows and latency SLOs; for low-latency scoring we use small batch sizes or no batching and rely on dedicated GPU throughput.
[07:10] Priya: for the POC can you trial both quantized 13B and a smaller 7B to see tradeoffs?
[07:14] Aaron: yes we'll include 7B/13B/70B variants in the benchmark and show cost/latency/regression metrics.
[07:20] David: security quick Q: SOC2 type 2, ISO, SSO, RBAC, and HSM for keys — all supported?
[07:26] Maya: yes SOC2 Type II and ISO are available for enterprise. we support SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging. we'll attach the security pack.
[07:34] Priya: we also need reproducible evals and regression alerts tied to our prompt sets.
[07:38] Aaron: Redwood Optimize has quality monitoring and regression alerts; we can tie to your evals.
[07:43] Maya: ok next steps recap: Aaron will run the bench with your prompt set (2k / 512) and simulate target concurrencies; Maya will send pricing and security docs; David will send prompt set and traffic pattern.
[07:55] David: sounds good, timeline is aggressive but this helps. any blockers on your side?
[08:00] Maya: none — we'll need credentials/secure upload for prompt set.
[08:05] Carlos: one more SRE question — can we pin model versions and do canary rollouts?
[08:09] Aaron: yes version pinning and rollouts are supported, canary, A/B, automatic fallback. logs/tracing for root cause.
[08:16] Priya: cost question — rough per-100k-token cost for dedicated vs hosted?
[08:20] Maya: i'll send a pricing sheet but dedicated is via reserved capacity and tends to be cheaper per token at scale; hosted charges per-token plus request overhead. we'll include a comparison.
[08:30] David: perfect. thanks everyone.
[08:33] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with docs and schedule POC scoping.

Notes on transcription: there are occasional mis-hears and shorthand (e.g., H100 spelled out as "H one hundred" in auto transcript), some proper names may be off.

End of call.
